content: Simultaneous testing for hepatitis A virus (HAV), hepatitis B core antigen (IgM anti-HBc), antibodies to hepatitis C virus (anti-HCV), and IgM antibodies to hepatitis E virus (IgM anti-HEV) is ideal to ensure no other types of viral hepatitis or co-infections are missed. However, sequential testing is often more cost-effective. Testing should ideally be provided free of charge to patients. If this is not possible within the healthcare system, funds must be allocated by investigators at sentinel sites to cover biomarker testing costs. National standard operating procedures (SOPs) will recommend specific algorithms and approved test kits based on sufficient sensitivity and specificity for each test included in the strategy. The working case definition for acute HCV infection, described as non-A, non-B, non-E acute hepatitis with positive HCV biomarkers, helps document trends in new HCV infections despite its imperfections. For example, in the United States, this definition was critical in identifying a recent outbreak of HCV infections linked to injection drug use after years of declining reported rates. In some countries, additional biomarkers not included in the WHO reference case definition may be routinely used. These may include fecal specimens for diagnosing HAV or HEV infections, IgG HEV, IgA HEV, and HEV RNA. In the absence of FDA-approved serological tests for diagnosing HEV infection, diagnostic methods vary between countries. While countries may use their own diagnostic tests per national guidelines, adopting WHO-recommended diagnostic algorithms facilitates international comparisons. Countries can adapt these SOPs and conduct analyses reflecting both national and WHO standards. Testing for hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection in patients with acute hepatitis may not be relevant in non-endemic countries. However, in highly endemic regions, HDV testing should be considered. At sentinel sites, only cases confirmed through biomarker testing will be included in the analysis. Enhanced case reporting requires high specificity to exclude chronic infections, which are more prevalent in the community. Cases meeting the presumptive acute hepatitis definition but testing negative for biomarkers will be excluded from the analysis. To avoid duplication, patients will be assigned unique identifiers or codes, which will be used on data collection forms and patient specimens. Hospital or national IDs can aid in this process while maintaining confidentiality. Initial interviews will screen for prior participation to prevent duplication. Databases will remain at sentinel sites and will not be shared, except for aggregated results as per data transmission protocols. Regular data analysis will track trends in case numbers by age, sex, and residence over time. It will also assess the proportion of patients exposed to potential risk factors for acute hepatitis A, B, C, and E. Collecting data on all risk factors from patients meeting case definitions will help generate hypotheses about transmission modes. For example, comparing confirmed cases of acute hepatitis B or C with hepatitis A cases can reveal differences in exposure frequencies, such as nosocomial exposure. However, this will not constitute a formal case-control study, which would be more suited for research than surveillance. Data will be transmitted annually to the national hepatitis control program for interpretation and action. WHO will facilitate the transmission of data from the Ministry of Health to analyze trends in acute hepatitis cases at the international level. This project focuses on establishing a new surveillance system for acute hepatitis, one of the three pillars of a national hepatitis surveillance system proposed by WHO. It is not considered research, as it does not aim to generate generalizable results. Investigators will ensure the protection of human subjects, as outlined below. Patients will benefit from accurate diagnoses and necessary counseling as part of routine healthcare. However, in countries with sentinel surveillance rather than nationwide systems, not all healthcare facilities may have access to this diagnostic capability. Patients will also be assessed for the risk of developing acute liver failure, and they will receive advice on avoiding risk factors, such as harmful medications, and when to seek hospitalization. Vaccination of household contacts for hepatitis A or B may also be recommended. Data analysis will identify risk factors for infection, guiding better prevention interventions for societal benefit. All approached subjects will benefit from biomarker testing, regardless of their participation in the project. Patients with acute hepatitis B or C will be advised to follow up to determine if they progress to chronic infection. Acute hepatitis C patients who do not clear the virus within six months will be eligible for treatment. Hepatitis A does not become chronic, while hepatitis E becomes chronic only in immunocompromised patients. Confidentiality will be maintained by using unique identifier codes instead of personal identifiers in electronic systems. The link between personal identifiers and codes will be securely stored. Information sheets will inform patients about the surveillance activity, its objectives, and the anonymous use of their data. Patients will be made aware of their right to withdraw their data and refuse participation. Dedicated investigators, not clinicians, will introduce the project to patients. An opt-out process will allow subjects to decline participation while still benefiting from free biomarker testing. The project involves routine clinical care and public health operations, and its eligibility for ethics committee clearance will depend on national and WHO determinations. Future projects implementing these SOPs with WHO support will require subsequent ethics reviews. Expected outputs include trends in acute hepatitis by type, center, age, and sex, as well as comparisons of risk factor exposure proportions during incubation periods. Expected outcomes include improved local prevention and control measures, capacity building for acute hepatitis surveillance, lessons for project expansion, and the creation of a community of practice among clinicians and laboratory specialists.
